Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
I played a deck with Protect Thine Own in the Baltimore/Glen Burnie
(Maryland, USA) tournament this past Saturday. I was hoping to actually
win the tournament to better be able to shout "in your face" on the
newsgroup today, but ended up "only" coming in third out of 20. :-)

The deck was based on getting an Inner Circle member and at least one
Prince or Justicar, all with Obf/Pre/Dom (mostly with For too, but I
didn't have deckspace to use that in this version). I think it's
noteworthy, too, that this deck was almost certainly not the best it
could have been: it was just modified a little from a stealth-vote deck
I already had to include four copies of Protect Thine Own (I had thought
I owned five of my own, but it turned out I only had three, and was only
able to borrow one on short notice).

I got game wins in all three preliminary games; in two of the three, I
would say Protect Thine Own was a major contributor to my doing well.
In the finals I chose my seat poorly. I was top seed and chose to sit
as Matt Morgan's prey, BJ Alton's predator, not realizing (a) that Matt
had Blessing of Chaos in his deck (and lucky for him drew it early on)
and (b) that Matt was probably, of the finalists, the most able to avoid
bringing out non-Camarilla vampires. (Every game I played had lots of
non-Camarilla targets; in the finals, everyone but me and Matt had
substantially non-Camarilla decks: in order around the table from me, it
was: IC/P/J Ventrue, Lasombra (Lucita/Marcus merging) bleed w/Anarchs,
!Malk/Malk stealth-bleed, Tzimisce bleed/block/War Ghoul, Malk/!Malk
stealth-bleed/block w/Protean.)

Here's what happened in my games.

Round 1: Got out Arika and later Marcus Vitel. Called Protect Thine
Own late in the game (was down to 2 players) to burn Le Dinh Tho. Had
vote lock most of the game (Lucita merged came out for grandprey early,
then Lucinde Alastor for predator, but then I got Marcus and reclaimed
vote dominance, and then predator was ousted). Got 4 of 5 VPs, ousting
Assamites, Lasombra, and Giovanni.

Round 2: Got out Lucinde Alastor and then Arika, very late in the game
Etrius as well. Switched seats with my prey to better use Parity Shifts
and try to escape from his Escaped Mental Patient (my only combat
defense was Obedience) - that didn't quite succeed as Lucinde did get
dunked, but since I was now his prey I could rescue before anyone (other
than him) got a chance to diablerize. Called two Protect Thine Owns
this game, relatively early against predator's Uncle George, and later
against my prey's Cailean (who had a Guardian Angel and Rack). I had
vote lock the whole game. Got 4 of 5 VPs, ousting Lasombra (new prey
after Dramatic Upheaval), missing chance to oust his prey with
Lasombra/Kiasyd because I didn't give him Parity Shift pool when I
should have, ousted !Nos "Cailean does it all" deck, ousted
original-prey (became predator after DU) Malk/!Malk stealth bleed.

Round 3: Got Arika, Marcus, and later in the game Leandro. Didn't get
any PTOs early, but when it was down to two players, called two of them
to burn my opponent's only two vampires (the same Malk/!Malk stealth
bleed as in round 2, this time he had only gotten Dolphin Black and
Uncle George; Uncle George had an Enchanted Marionette and Dolphin had a
Pulse of the Canaille). That sealed the game in my favor; I had ousted
a Daughters/!Toreador vote deck earlier and got 3 VPs by also ousting
the !Malks, who had the other 2 VPs from ousting um... I wanna say a
Ventrue deck, he might've had Lucinde Alastor?, and then my predator, a
Harbingers/Giovanni (?) deck with Slaughterhouses and stuff.

Final round: Got Arika. Called an early Protect Thine Own on my prey's
Lucita (the same player as the Lasombra bleed in the first round), but
was low on pool due to his first-turn Anarch Revolt and later
Antediluvian Awakening, as well as my predator's having bled some. Got
ousted after having to burn Arika to the Antediluvian, not having
managed to gain any pool yet.

In every game I played, I had vote lock most of the time if not all the
time. On several occasions, I didn't need to play any card besides the
Protect Thine Own to call and pass the vote. I burned a total of 39
capacity of vampires with 6 Protect Thine Owns, an average of 6.5
capacity (there were larger targets available in some cases but wanting
to hit my predator or prey first I wasn't going to choose the
cross-table ones). I had to apologize every time I called one because I
felt unclean for playing the card. :-)

Josh

push in play to pass it, instead of Arika who would not have been able

playable if my predator, Matt, had attempted (despite failing) the block

transferred 11 or 15 pool (I'm not sure if I had made 4 transfers after

It does show that my seating choice turned out to be poor, probably, and
that Matt was both lucky and good in that game.

> Still a good performance though, congrats.

Thanks. Obviously four games aren't going to convince most of the
people on the "PTO is just fine" side, but I think it's at least some
good data on how strong the effect of PTO typically is, and how low the
cost of playing it can be.

I guess this is as good a place as any to interject.

There are cards that bother me because they are overpowered such that they
screw up the competitive level of the game. Then, there are other cards that
bother me, sometimes more, because their effect is too great *and* because they
don't see consistent enough play. PTO goes into the latter category. Why can
it be worse when a card is only "unfair" some of the time? What's strong and
ubiquitous gets metagamed against. What's only situationally strong often
isn't worth metagaming against because "there are no wrong threats, only wrong
answers" - you can't metagame against everything that might hurt you and still
be playing your game. Cards like PTO, powerful hosers, and the like produce an
environment where you get *randomly* totally screwed.

So, I think I understand what this current argument, that mainly Josh is
making, is trying to get at. That the card only affects some decks reduces its
power, but it makes it a more random and, thus, unfair (in a particular usage
of unfair) card with a high power effect. If War Ghoul could only rush
non-Cams, it would be weaker, but it would be more of a hoser and less
something that you would metagame against because it would see less play
overall, which would have the tendency of making decks more vulnerable to being
screwed by it.

> vampires on the table can even damage a warghoul, even without taking
> memories of martality into account. Suppose you play vote or bleed :
> do you prefer loose a vampire or get rushed by a warghoul every turn ?

I'd prefer getting rushed, honestly. War Ghouls you can defend against
with your combat defense (just ask Matt Morgan) that you already want to
play with because combat happens every game. And you might be able to
steal them with Dominate, Presence, Dementation, or Serpentis (am I
missing anything?). And even if all that fails, you can get rescued
from torpor on your own or by your allies. Once your vampire is burned
by PTO, trying to recover means investing another big chunk of pool in
trying to bring out a replacement before you get ousted.

I absolutely agree that War Ghoul and Palla Grande are very strong cards
and on the top of their respective power curves. But I don't think they
have as much of a negative impact on the game as a whole as Protect
Thine Own does, largely because they work much more in the framework of
"established standard effects that are common to every game of VTES".
(That is, getting in combat with scary combat minions and getting bled
for more than 1, both of which are very typical things that a huge
number of common decks do, and which can be accomplished in many
practical ways. Getting your vampire burned by a vote, on the other
hand, is not a standard effect available to lots of decks, and trying to
defend effectively against it requires a very specific set of cards that
aren't applicable to as wide a range of "these come up every VTES game"
type of effects.)

Josh
